# Top 5 posts from r/MovieSuggestions day

## 1. Looking for heartbreaking movies where one (or both) of the leads die

**Score:** 75
**Body:** I'm in the mood to get emotionally wrecked. 😭

Please recommend movies where at least one of the main leads (hero or heroine) dies. Bonus points if both of them do. I'm not looking for shock value though. I want good storytelling, strong direction, and characters that make you deeply invested before ripping my heart out.

Romance doesn't have to be the main plot, but I'd love it if the emotional payoff is worth it. No spoilers beyond the fact that one of the leads dies, please. Thank you!

### Top 10 comments and their replies (up to depth 10)

1. Romeo + Juliet (1996)


2. What dreams may come. I sob through the whole damn movie. Especially now with robin williams dead, it hits so much harder. 
3. My Girl (1991)
4. *Life is Beautiful*
5. Steel Magnolias
6. Leaving Las Vegas (1995)
7. Philadelphia
8. Brokeback Mountain. Cried so much. 
9. Titanic (1997)

All dogs go to heaven (1989)
10. The Green Mile

# Top 5 posts from r/moviecritic day

## 1. Mad Max Fury Road is a 10/10 Masterpiece. George Miller is a genius.

**Score:** 535
**Body:** just had the chance to rewatch this movie. i always find new things to love/appreciate about it. Watching the action sequences back, i legitimately cannot believe the majority of the movie was shot using practical effects. Action aside, the story and world building are exceptionally done as well. The movie is also incredibly gorgeous, with every frame being so carefully curated, every shot is like a painting. The vastness of creativity is so remarkable, I’ll never get tired of this movie, and it was time for my ritualistic rewatch of this. Anyway, this is your sign from the universe to go rewatch fury road today.

### Top 7 comments and their replies (up to depth 10)

1. In an interview Miller said he wanted the visual language of the film to be so strong that a non english speaking viewer could watch the film and understand every second of it even without subtitles. Not sure if he 100% accomplished that goal but I am 100% sure that's an amazing way to think about composing a film
  - I full believe that, because I'm a full English speaker, however my local cinema had the worst audio system so the dialogue was gibberish to me, but I still had one of the best cinema experiences ever without it. 

I honestly didn't even know the bad guy's name or that it was anything close to "Immortan Joe" until I watched it at home a year later. 
  - Thank you for this 
2. Best action movie of the last 10 years at least.
  - Ever. Best action movie ever. Nothing gets my heart pumping like that movie. When I saw it in theaters after the opening chase into the sandstorm my heart was pumping so hard I actively had to calm myself down.
3. The scene where they enter the sand storm and you can see tornadoes inside and the music is blasting gives me chills every time 
4. I worked in VFX compositing and post conversion on this one. This was definitely one of those, “every shot is a painting” films for me. Our work is literally frame by frame a lot of the time and this was one where that wasn’t a slog at all. Gorgeous film. Amazing editing. Simple well executed story and concept. It’s a perfect movie. 
5. Love this film.

Two years back I saw a "crome" version on a visit to Seattle.

The lack of color made the film less powerful for me. It was an interesting viewing, but the drab color of the post-apocolyptic Max world is important.
6. His wife deserves some credit too, she did most of the editing and came into the movie without the action movie mindset and everything is better for it. If it were handled like action movies were in the late 2000's and early 2010's, it would have been much less of a masterpiece and just a good Mad Max movie with a thousand jump cuts. 
  - It was a combo; Margaret Sixel deservedly won the Oscar for her editing, while her husband set her up for success by center framing the action in all of the action shots, so your eye could follow what was happening, even with quick cuts.

## 5. Ryan Gosling and Project Hail Mary reminded me why hope still matters in science fiction.

**Score:** 138
**Body:** In a world increasingly fascinated by nihilism, cynicism, and darkness, Project Hail Mary quietly argues the opposite. It reminds us that hope is born through genuine connection, and that the strongest bonds are forged not through similarity, but through surviving the impossible together.  
With *The Odyssey* and *Spider-Man* dominating the conversation, I know I’m probably one of the last people to watch *Project Hail Mary*. But films like this deserve to be revisited long after the excitement fades, because they leave something behind. They linger.  
I could spend this review talking about the breathtaking cinematography, the beautiful score, or Ryan Gosling’s performance. This was actually the first film of his I’ve ever watched, and it certainly won’t be the last. His ability to move seamlessly between comedy and drama makes Ryland Grace feel remarkably human.  
Yet none of that is what stayed with me the most.  
What truly stayed with me was the bond that emerged from survival.  
Grace and Rocky have almost nothing in common. They belong to different species, speak different languages, perceive the universe differently, and are fundamentally incompatible on a biological level. Rocky survives in an ammonia-rich atmosphere that would kill a human, while oxygen, the very thing that keeps humans alive, is poisonous to him. By every law of nature, they were never meant to understand each other.  
And yet, they do.  
Not because they share the same world, but because they share the same catastrophe.  
Together, they endure the crushing loneliness of deep space, shoulder the impossible responsibility of saving their worlds, and witness one another fail, adapt, learn, and persevere. Every challenge they overcome becomes another layer of trust, until that trust evolves into something far greater than friendship.  
The film’s most powerful moment isn’t a scientific breakthrough or an awe inspiring visual.  
It’s Rocky’s instinct to save Grace.  
Without hesitation, he is willing to sacrifice himself for someone who isn’t even a member of his own species. He chooses to do for Grace what he could never do for his own people. Even after spending 183 years with his mate, the bond forged through shared hardship becomes so profound that, in that moment, nothing matters more than saving the friend who faced the impossible beside him.  
The film then mirrors that sacrifice perfectly.  
Grace, a man with no one waiting for him on Earth, chooses to leave humanity behind in order to save the one companion who stood beside him through every impossible moment. He gives up his chance to return home because, somewhere along the journey, Rocky became home.  
That single decision says more about friendship than pages of dialogue ever could.  
*Project Hail Mary* reminded me that friendship, and perhaps every meaningful relationship, isn’t built on words, appearances, or superficial similarities. It is built through shared hardship, mutual trust, and the quiet understanding that only those who survive the same storm can truly know one another.  
Maybe that’s why this film affected me so deeply.  
At its core, *Project Hail Mary* isn’t simply a story about saving Earth.  
It’s a story about two souls separated by every imaginable difference, proving that the strongest bond in the universe isn’t created by blood, language, or even biology, but by surviving the impossible together.

# Top 5 posts from r/TrueFilm day

## 1. 30 for 30. My breakdown of the best 30 Japanese movies of the last 30 years, with reviews for each.

**Score:** 147
**Body:** I’ve spent the last 18 months deep diving into modern Japanese cinema. I’ve always known about the classics (Miyazaki, Beat Takeshi, Miike etc.) but I’ve never actually sat down and thoroughly consumed it more broadly. After doing so, I have a pretty good idea of what the best 30 films of the last 30 years are.

When you deep dive like this, you start to notice patterns between films. The same themes - alienation, societal norms, unanswered family tensions, school pains, dissatisfied wives - crop up again and again. It's fun to see different films approach these themes in different ways.

I acknowledge that my list is missing a fair few names. Here are a few that didn't quite make the cut:

The Taste of Tea, Ringu, Ichii the Killer, Adrift in Tokyo, Still Walking, Like Father Like Son, Wheel of Fortune & Fantasy, Cold Fish, Why Don't You Play in Hell?, The Girl Who Leapt Through Time, Perfect Blue, Departures, Dead or Alive, One Million Yen Girl, and Love & Pop.

My list starts at 1995 and ends in 2024 (I’m cheating a little by not including 2025 and because I really wanted to include two 1995 films here). This is the best 30 Japanese movies of the last 30 years in my view. Let me know what you've seen, what you agree with, and what you don't.

1. **Love Exposure (2008) Sion Sono**

Love Exposure, simply put, is the War & Peace of extreme cinema. It’s the kind of movie you can’t possibly be indifferent to. I came out of my first screening of this movie in a state of genuine delirium. I knew I had witnessed something truly profound while at the same time utterly ridiculous. The sheer audacity of a filmmaker to think they can make a movie about an upskirt photographer who gets entangled in a web of religious sin, wacky cults, and uniquely Japanese sexual perversion, and to make the story 4-hours no less (down from the original 6-hour cut), is truly staggering. And yet the whole thing works. It never sags. It never feels glib or mismatched. And despite the obvious absurdity of the entire thing, there is a genuine purity and innocence to it all, which raises a crucial question: Where does love start and perversion end? 

**2. Eureka (2000) Shinji Aoyama**

Eureka is a sepia-toned character study about the lasting effects of a violent rampage on its only survivors - a bus driver and two teenage siblings who were riding it that morning. It’s a movie that unravels at a simmering pace. At a demanding 217 minutes, it’s not a movie for the impatient. The manifestation of the tragedy’s effects on these characters are hinted at subtly. We see small snippets. The children stop speaking altogether. The bus driver attempts, somewhat clumsily, to build a simple routine. It’s a fascinating insight into how trauma can induce a numbness to the world, or a guilt for surviving it. But also something far more sinister, where the urge to be violent manifests in the victims of it. It’s a demanding watch, but an incredibly rewarding and perceptive one.

**3. Cure (1997) Kiyoshi Kurosawa**

A great horror movie will frighten you, a good one will scare you, and a bad one, if lucky, will just gross you out. It is rare, however, for a movie, any movie, to truly get under your skin. Kurosawa’s Cure, a tale about a hapless police detective attempting to solve a string of similar killings going up against a seemingly amnesiac mesmerist, is one of the creepiest films ever put to celluloid. What starts off as a police procedural and murder mystery becomes something more akin to a chilling social critique of Japanese society and a deep dive into the world of mesmerism. It’s never really about who is doing the murders, but rather what the murders say about people deep down inside, and what they’re truly capable of. Eerily spine-chilling from start to finish. 

**4. Spirited Away (2001) Hayao Miyazaki** 

So much has already been written about Spirited Away, and more broadly Miyazaki, that it almost feels redundant adding to it here. All I can really say is that Spirited Away feels like the closest realisation to what you might explain a Ghibli movie to someone who for whatever reasons appears to have lived under a rock on Mars for the last 30 years. Explaining the details of the plot of this story of a young girl seemingly getting trapped in a magical realm while her parents transform into pigs is missing the point. This movie is all journey, all experience, and all image. It is a movie well-aware of the power of the image, and how that can be used to explore the young feelings of alienation, fear, and loneliness adolescents feel as they attempt to navigate a scary new world. And it does so without ever patronising its audience. You feel very much like it's on the same level. 

**5. Love Letter (1995) Shinji Awai** 

A widow looking for closure writes a letter to her deceased husband’s former address. She is shocked when she gets a response from someone responding to the same name. And thus begins an emotional exploration into the life of the man who died in the snow 2 years before, but whose memories still glisten in its reflection for two identical-looking women he previously loved. It’s a brilliant conceit, and one used to explore who someone may or may not have been through the memories of others. But also how we can see memories differently as we grow despite them seemingly remaining unchanged. Love Letter is a romance film in its truest sense. The characters think, feel, and grow through the romances they had, and the movie shows how exploring someone’s life through the words of others can help them to move on. I specifically wanted to start my journey in 1995 just to make sure this movie made the list. 

**6. Battle Royale (2000) Kinji Fukusaku** 

Battle Royale’s cultural legacy has spawned an entire realm of similarly themed entities all unto themselves, whether it’s deathmatch video games like PUBG or the much-heralded Hunger Games series of books and films. And yet despite all this, the film still feels bold and original today. It’s a film told with rousing verve and energy, combining elements of action-adventure, political satire, and slapstick comedy. The director Kinji Fukatsu said he was inspired to adapt the novel of the story because he remembered working in a munitions factory during world war two, and having to hide under the bodies of other fellow worker-students as the factory came under fire by the US navy. It built in him a hatred and general distrust of what adults tell kids about the world. Battle Royale is the manifestation of that general distrust. The idea that the world may not have your best interests at heart despite what it’s trying to tell you. 

**7. Drive My Car (2021) Ryusuke Hamaguchi**

Ryusuke Hamaguchi’s utterly beautiful film Drive My Car is an epic meditation on grief, and the uncomfortable truths around disintegrating relationships and what might have been. A recently-widowed playwright is assigned a driver to take him to his workshop every day, and a slow bond around shared loss and grief forms between them as they delicately reveal more about themselves. As in many of his other films, we see entire segments play out in real time, car journeys, play scenes, conversations at bars, and are forced to feel the changing emotional tides in real time, as the characters would have. It’s a movie that slowly takes us under the car hood and shows us what has worn down over time. And how the repression of these feelings can peel away when your guard is lowered. But hopefully, the airing out of these feelings can help you move on. A movie that truly earned its 3-hour length. 

**8. Audition (1999) Takashi Miike** 

Takashi Miike is maybe Japan’s most fascinating filmmaker. With over 100 direction credits under his belt, you’d be forgiven for not knowing where to start with his work. He’s done everything from formulaic gangster flicks to genre-defying fever dreams. Audition is the best of both worlds. The story of a middle aged widower staging fake auditions to find himself a girlfriend positions itself at first as an offbeat romantic comedy, and then very much as an excruciating horror show in its second half. The less said about the latter the better. It’s that transition that best sums up Miike’s mastery of his craft. He’s able to meld two distinctly opposite genres so seamlessly to create something instantly classic and all the more terrifying for it. 

**9. All About Lily Chou Chou (2001) Shunji Iwai**

I wasn’t sure how I’d feel about this movie, since it still divides people now. But the longer AALCC went on, the more engrossed I became. It’s not just a gut-wrenching exploration of school day trauma, bullying, and youthful alienation. It’s the overlaying of that with 1. An exploration of the world of proto-social media, 2. A non-linear narrative interspersed with said messages, and 3. The music of the titular character. Both the music and the message boards offer an escape for our protagonist Hasumi as he tries to find solace away from the grim sadism of his tormentor, his once-friend Hoshino. As the movie goes on, it becomes clear that both boys are living through torment for different reasons, but deal with it differently - Hoshino through rage and the control of others and Hasumi through passive acceptance and a numbness to the world. And while the music of Lily Chou Chou and the internet provide both with brief respite from their pain, neither is a cure for it. 

**10. Your Name. (2016) Makoto Shinkai** 

This visually stunning anime about two high schoolers from different parts of the country, who start body-swapping after waking up, completely captivated, stunned, and exhausted me. Its central premise is enough of a selling point - that a comet is hurtling to earth and might seem to have something to do with this magical happenstance. But what really reeled me in was the ability of the film to put me in the mind of its two heroes. When Mitsuha screamed of wishing to be a boy from the city, I suddenly felt that same frustration despite having lived my entire life in big cities. It’s a film with a strong sense of place and purpose, even though the director Makoto Shinkai has often expressed dissatisfaction with how the film turned out. Every dreamlike thought that is expressed in the film feels like it's inches away from being buried at the bottom of one’s id if they aren’t fought for and rescued. There are lots of ways to see the film. I feel like it’s about how the linearity of time matters less than the marks that are made along the way. Memories may fade, details may become unclear, but the emotions that were felt will always be very clear.

**11. Princess Mononoke (1997) Hayao Miyazaki** 

The second Ghibli movie on this list, but could also easily be the first, Princess Mononoke takes the epic scope and sweeping visuals of Nausicaa but adds a contemporary issue - the very real clash between nature and development, and the folly of human hubris that enables it. The visuals are typically flawless, with lush, sweeping hand-drawn landscapes, and the characters themselves are rich and complex. As would be a common hallmark of Miyazaki, we also have a strong female lead who embodies the wounded resistance to the exploitation of the forest. It is an endlessly rewatchable film too, giving you something extra each time to go over and debate, or just sit back and enjoy. 

**12. Nobody Knows (2004) Hirokatsu Koreeda**

What I admire most about the incredible filmmaker Koreeda is how his entire oeuvre feels like a collective study of what it truly means to be a family, and even more broadly than that, to find real humanity outside the boundaries of familial orthodoxy. None of his films feel quite as tragic or doomerist as this one. Rather than a celebration of and re-thinking of the family unit, this is a study of what happens when children are left to fend for themselves. There is still the desire to play and discover the world together, but without the guardrails families provide, basic needs are harder to find and danger becomes more pronounced. No movie has ever been as easily sympathetic as this one. Every scene, replete with (or perhaps in spite of) stoic down-to-earth kitchen-sink realism, is utterly compelling. 

**13. Haru (1996) Yoshimitsu Morita**

The second movie on this list that deals with online relationships. Perhaps it's fitting that this is also a movie that deals with the early days of the internet, and the way it incentivises people to pepper their lives with embellishments. But more than that, also how it provided safe spaces for lonely and misplaced people to connect with each other. I think the most memorable and interesting aspect of this film is how it attempts to cinematise the exchanging of emails. Unlike movies that would come later like All About Lily Chou Chou and the Korean drama Please Take Care of My Cat, this movie displayed them in a more subdued style. Fragments of the male and female protagonists’ lives are interspersed with their online posts, some of them genuine and heartfelt, others hyperbolic or downright false. But ultimately, this depiction of digitalised love, intimacy, and human connection is no less real. The characters really do care for each other. It’s just that along with that comes the perverse incentive to pretend you’re someone else. 

**14. Kotoko (2011) Shinya Tsukamoto** 

In this highly intimate psychological horror movie, J-Pop idol Cocco’s electrifying performance as a single mother struggling with mental illness takes the audience through a harrowing whirlwind of hallucinations, nervous breakdowns and self-harm.The extreme close-ups, disjointed editing, and sickly pink-and-yellow colour palette firmly place you into Kotoko’s unravelling psyche. The only solace she seems to find amid her mental collapse is in a family visit with her son and in soulful, emotionally fragile bursts of song peppered throughout the movie. We are never entirely sure what we are seeing is what is actually happening, but what is for sure is that Tsukamoto’s depiction of mental illness feels as painfully true to life as anything I’ve seen before or since. 

**15. Harmonium (2016) Koji Fukada** 

A man hires an old acquaintance to assist him in his workshop. He also settles in the family’s spare room and strikes up an emotional connection to his friend’s wife. It’s quickly clear that things are off and not is all it seems. Our first clue as to things feeling sinister is in the introductory shot of the quietly intense Tadanobu Asano’s character. It is almost Haneke-esque in its slow unravelling of past issues bubbling up unresolved, and the ramifications they wield. It’s also an example of a movie that takes one direction in the first half, and completely changes course in the second. But ultimately this isn’t a movie about conclusions. It’s about the fruitless search for them. “I just want to know what happened,” the husband says to his wife. “What difference would it make?”. Fukada isn’t interested in answering the question so easily for us. 

**16. Howl’s Moving Castle (2004) Hayao Miyazaki** 

It was challenging to know which Ghibli movies to fit in here, but Howl’s Moving Castle is a worthy addition to the list. It’s a movie that makes me wish I could temporarily be Japanese so that the themes might resonate more deeply with me. Japan being a country that is constantly wrestling with its own self-identity, perhaps Sophie’s transformation would feel all the more poignant. But it isn’t just a movie about the individual, it's also about wrestling with the idea that war always poisons the seeming nobility of it. About how magic, rather than purely being good or evil, has the capacity for both. And also about how courage isn’t simply about heroism, but rather the impetus to act despite what dangers may be lurking. There are so many other things I could mention that couldn’t possibly fit into one paragraph. And as you might expect from a Ghibli movie, every frame is as richly beautiful as the next. 

**17. Paprika (2006) Satoshi Kon**

A time-bending romp through cyberpunk Japan, Paprika has influenced a mighty list of heavy-hitters (Inception being the obvious one). But regardless of what came later, Kon movies still feel effortlessly unique. He is a filmmaker who seems to fully understand that the confines of traditional scene transitions can be innovated through animation. Characters seemingly jump from streets into billboards, one character walks into frame with another suddenly leaving, and before you know it, you’re three or four dreams deep inside the film. But this doesn’t simply act as a technical flourish. We are watching a master of his craft tell stories in a uniquely bold and brilliant way. Even if it’s hard to fully grasp the narrative at first, the characters still feel like people we can relate to (even if we’re not quite sure who is or isn’t real). 

**18. Shoplifters (2018) Hirokazu Koreeda** 

What is more important? Blood relations or genuine care and compassion? It seems like such an obvious question, but very often it’s blood that takes precedence. Koreeda’s subjects are a loosely assembled group of people who for all intents and purposes, act as a family. The father and son have a perfected routine of stealing from their local shops in order to feed and house themselves, and rationalise it by saying that items can’t be stolen since they “haven’t been bought yet”. But this is just one aspect of the film. What Koreeda is really interested in is the idea of what it really means to be a family. The people in this film steal not because they want to but because of their poor circumstances. Yet despite this, they seem relatively happy and lucky to have each other. The youngest member Yuri, who they find neglected on a porch outside in the cold, is welcomed in by them and treated as their own. It’s a movie that contrasts the legality and social definition of family with the true act of love. The characters might steal, but ultimately what they’re looking for is warmth, stability and love in a society that can’t provide those through law. 

**19. Guilty of Romance (2011) Sion Sono** 

This dark and unadulterated erotic thriller is one for the ages. Seeking to break free of the confines of mundane domestic Japanese wifehood, a woman named Izumi embarks on a scintillating but perilous sexual journey, first through magazine shoots but then eventually to street sex work. She’s guided through this journey by multiple fascinating characters, but mostly by Mitsuko, a lecturer by day and streetwalker by night. At the same time, a female detective named Yoshida, herself engaging in an illicit love affair, seems to be investigating the circumstances around a violent crime scene set in Tokyo’s sexual underworld. This latter plotline, while perhaps the movie’s overwrought weakpoint, nevertheless infuses the film with an uncomfortable tension that makes us think something horrible is eventually going to happen. Guilty of Romance is essential viewing for a number of reasons, but the real joy of it is the characters themselves. Mitusko, partly based on a real life person, is one of the most fascinating personalities I’ve ever seen on screen. All three women act as their own rebellions against the confines of traditional societal roles for wives and women. But the journeys they take, while empowering in a sense, are not ones of success or happiness. They are ultimately about the true cost of agency in a world that wants to rid them of it. 

**20. Swing Girls (2004) Sinobu Yaguchi** 

Swing Girls might be the most purely fun film on this list. The story of a band of misfits with no music backgrounds coming together to form a brass band is filled with visual comic set pieces, funny lines, and plenty of toe-tapping tunes to get you in the mood. My list is filled with movies that ruminate on the loneliness epidemic Japan seems to’ve been going through for decades now, so it’s nice to find a film about a group of people seeming to solve their own. While the plot itself is fairly formulaic, the film’s joy comes from the characters themselves and the energy they generate from each other. At no point does the film feel trite. The girls are endearing and funny, the journey they go on is rip-roaringly entertaining, and the film itself continues to be effortlessly rewatchable even after 20 years. Ultimately there isn’t a single message to take away here. It’s a laugh riot that’s all about the journey and not the destination. 

**21. Noriko’s Dinner Table (2005) Sion Sono** 

A prequel to the 2001 thriller Suicide Club, Noriko’s Dinner Table is a film that explores how the strong East Asian insistence on familial piety coupled with formality can lead to alienation and a yearning for self-identity. Eldest daughter Noriko abandons her family to seek her own with an online acquaintance. She is soon joined by her younger sister. The father decides to try and find out where they are. Unlike other Sono films, this one is distinctly less sexually lurid and blood-splattery. Like other Sono films, it is filled with utterly memorable characters and a pace that jumps from riproaring to slow burning with equal aplomb. It’s also just as intense and stylish as you’d expect a Sono film to be, and demands to be seen more than once to fully grasp the themes and questions it raises. Imagine completely abandoning one life to start another? Can you truly reset yourself this way? And even if you could, are you any happier for it? 

**22. Happy Hour (2015) Ryuchi Hamaguchi** 

This 5-hour+ character drama about 3 women all at different crossroads in their domestic lives is a truly rewarding watch for those who dare to take the time to do so. Four female friends question whether their lives are going where they want them to when one of them reveals herself to be having an affair and seeking a divorce. An extraordinary thing about this film is how entire sections of it seem to play out in real time. One sequence, in which our 4 protagonists attend an alternative therapy section, plays out for nearly an hour. In the hands of a less capable filmmaker, it might be pushing the limits of watchability, but here the payoffs to each section feel warmly earned. At no point is it boring. It may be a slow burn by the standards of some of the films on this list, but there’s something purely cinematic about watching conversations that would ordinarily play out in a few cuts, stay on screens for much longer. We are forced to sit there and feel the awkwardness when conversations become tense or uncomfortable. We aren’t served with convenient cuts so that we can then ruminate on what just happened. Characters get angry, and then stay angry, and the fallout remains. What is all the more amazing is that the film is carried by 4 captivating actresses who’d never acted in a full length feature film before. 

**23. Ghost in the Shell (1995) Mamoru Oshii** 

Although perhaps not quite as beloved as the electrifying Akira, or as culturally significant as the best of Studio Ghibli, Oshii’s 1995 cyberpunk thriller is still a thrilling, visually striking benchmark of 1990s anime. Even now it boasts enduring admiration and fandom, with its complex themes of individuality, human agency, and the boundaries of technology. And who could forget the incredible theme song? The philosophical musings of the characters may come across as slightly clunky and on-the-nose, but there’s still so much here to justify multiple viewings. It’s a splendid mix of what-does-it-mean-to-be-human thoughts, morbidly dystopian cityscapes, and slick action. 

**24. Linda Linda Linda (2004) Nubohiro Yamashita**

The scene that best sums up this delightfully quirky high school film is when one boy character professes his love to Bae Doona’s Korean exchange student. “I don’t dislike you but I don’t like you either” she replies. “I want to be with my friends.” Linda Linda Linda is a movie about a group of friends who form a band and slowly learn how to play the songs of punk band Blue Heart together, at first disjointedly, eventually harmoniously, but always with verve, passion and fun. It isn’t about people falling in love. It isn’t about people growing and discovering themselves. It isn’t about discovering the meaning of life. It isn’t about escaping some traumatic home life. It’s a movie about the small things we do, as youngsters, that don’t feel like it in the moment, but actually define the old John Lennon adage of “Life is what happens to you when you’re busy making other plans.” These girls meet for practice, they learn how to play together, occasionally they do things related to their school or home lives, but the music is always in the forefront of their minds. It’s remarkable that the film feels both offbeat yet remarkably sincere. I guess it’s this fusion that best sums up the awkwardness of school life. 

**25. Tokyo Sonata (2008) Kiyoshi Kurosawa** 

Kurosawa is best known for his forays into Japanese horror. But here we see him operating at a much different scale. Tokyo Sonata is about the ever growing cracks in the foundation of the ideal Japanese family. The stiff-upper-lipped dad is laid off from his job, and spends his days looking for work and hanging out in small parks with his fellow recently-made-redundant suits. He forbids his youngest son from playing the piano, so the youngster begins taking lessons in secret. His wife, ever yearning for a more loving relationship, begins to imagine life differently, perhaps even elsewhere. It’s a movie that explores the tension between what society expects and what people actually want. Everyone in the film knows that their lives are slowly slipping away, and it’s a constant struggle to maintain the facade. It’s a theme that pops up again and again in Japanese cinema, but few films have explored it as well or in as much detail as Tokyo Sonata. 

**26. A Silent Voice (2016) Naoko Yamada** 

Whereas all the other animes on this list deal with cyberpunk dystopias, magical realms, or supernatural twists of fate, A Silent Voice is the lone wolf anime here of grounded reality, albeit one with an incredible inventive visual style. This is a tale of a young bully Ishida coming to try and atone for his past behaviour by befriending his deaf former victim, Shuoko. Ishida is shunned by his peers after they blame him for her transferring schools. His subsequent alienation is represented by each classmate having an X on their face, as he can’t bear to look them in the eyes. There are many visual cues throughout the movie, many that I’ve yet to fully decode myself. There is a lot of flowery imagery connected to each character. The visual style helps to guide us through what the characters are feeling. It’s a movie that combines a keen visual style with outstanding writing, so that the characters and setting feel very much alive and vibrant. 

**27. 0.5mm (2016) Mamoko Ando**

Mamoko Ando’s 3-hour dramedy about a care-worker extorting her way into the employment of one old man after another has a fascinating structure. It starts out with a series of quirky but darkly comic errors that lead to our protagonist’s hapless unemployed state. After that initial shock, we then enjoy her rambunctious attempts to extort the more side-eyingly creepy behaviour of her geriatric targets. Each meeting slowly turns into a caring and heartwarming codependency - but with each meeting adding a few more heartstrings than the last. But her forceful extortion attempts aren’t simply a comedic device. They serve to highlight the struggles of old age, how agency becomes harder to retain in the face of failing bodies, predatory scammers, and a largely indifferent society. Somewhere lost in that shuffle, is the deeply affecting touch of humanity that Sakura Ando’s character enables both her and her targets to once again feel. 

**28. Like Someone in Love (2012) Abbas Kiarostami** 

The only film in this list made by a foreigner, Iran’s Abbas Kiarostami, *Like Someone in Love* is a film that deals with its themes cryptically. We’re never quite sure if the conversations being had, the points being made, or the story details that emerge actually serve any kind of narrative purpose. All we really know for sure is the people on screen, Akiko the secret sex worker, her jealous boyfriend, and her elderly professor-cum-client, all seem deeply unsure of who they are and where they’re going. They also struggle to express this, and often confuse each other. It’s a film that looks at relationship dynamics, both broadly but also within the context of patriarchal Japan, and asks what it truly means to “be in love”. They each seem to be lying to each other in order to keep the facade going. Not that it saves them. 

**29. Harmful Insect (2001) Akihiko Shiota** 

Another film that depicts the alienation of Japan’s youth, here we have a movie with a largely mute and disassociated school girl named Sachiko who deals with her life struggles by skipping school and exploring her neighbourhood with local vagabonds. Her father has abandoned the family, and her mother, largely absent, has attempted suicide. Her only refuge seems to be an exchange of letters with a former school teacher of hers. We don’t know the nature of their relationship but it is rumoured around school that he had a love affair with Sachiko. Harmful Insect joins Haru and All About Lily Chou-Chou as a film that deals with disaffected and isolated people who find their feelings through words - in this case letters. Sachiko lives an aimless existence. She doesn’t pursue any dreams or have any goals. She merely learns to cope with her dreadful circumstances. Every adult around her either seems predatory or equally discarded. It’s not a film about finding solutions, but one about highlighting problems. 

**30. Suicide Club (2001) Sion Sono** 

Suicide Club is ¾’s an engrossing mystery, and ¼ a hot mess. But even though the film is uneven and impossible to pin down, my fascination with what it all means remains with me to this day. I spent days trying to figure out what the message was after my first viewing, why people were casually choosing to kill themselves, and how this was related to the changing digital tides of early 2000s Japan. What is very clear to me is that the good here is very good. It’s a movie with a sharp horror sensibility that shifts tones both abruptly but also effortlessly. The themes are not obvious but they are very fun to engage with and debate. If nothing else, it’s a movie that takes you down a dark and unpredictable road and invites you to enjoy the ride even if the destination isn’t necessarily where you paid to go.

## 2. The Aviator made me realize why Nolan doesn’t hold a candle to Scorsese

**Score:** 150
**Body:** Finally got around to filling in one of my last blanks in Scorsese’s filmography. It was sort of funny watching *The Aviator* in the midst of Nolan-mania, with everyone (including yours truly) offering their two cents on his version of ”Great Man” cinema. To me, it\* \*seems like the sort of movie Nolan thinks he made with *Oppenheimer* and, in some ways, *The Odyssey*. What sets Scorsese apart, however, is that, while there is certainly identification with the subject, there is far less reverence. Nolan’s troubled geniuses often feel flat to me because whatever their faults, I’m ultimately always expected to admire them—and by extension Nolan himself, alongside the sheer scale of his accomplishment. Less so with Marty’s deeply fucked up, perverted misfits. I’d like to see Nolan have one of his protagonists lock himself naked in a movie theater surrounded by milk bottles full of piss. Or try to make movies like *Alice Doesn’t Live Here Anymore* or *The Age of Innocence,* for that matter.

Scorsese certainly has a point of view, but he directs it outward. Travis Bickle, Jake La Motta, Jordan Belfort and Howard Hughes all have traits in common, and yet they are far more diverse than the likes of John Cobb, Bruce Wayne, Oppenheimer and Odysseus. Really I think it boils down to curiosity about something other than the self. Nolan uses his art to come to grips with his own obsessions and neuroses, Scorsese tries to understand the world around him. I sure know which of the two I find more interesting.

Edit: Just wanted to add that I don’t hate Nolan nor any of his films. I like both Oppenheimer and The Odyssey just fine. I wrote this mainly because I feel like the media has been so Nolan-heavy lately (understandably so), that it was such a breath of fresh air to go back and watch a Scorsese joint. It just so happened to align thematically with a lot of Nolan’s stuff, and so I inevitably found myself making the comparison.

Both directors are attracted to men who build something massive and then get eaten alive by it, Scorsese is just dirtier about it and Nolan is more controlled. That’s a difference in temperament, not proof that one has depth and the other doesn’t.  
also the “i’d like to see Nolan make *Alice Doesn’t Live Here Anymore*” point is always such a weird argument. Okay? I’d like to see Scorsese make *Dunkirk*. I’d like to see him build *Memento* around its structure without the whole thing collapsing. Directors aren’t better because they could hypothetically make somebody else’s movies. Scorsese has a wider emotional register in some areas, Nolan has formal abilities Scorsese has never really shown much interest in. That’s fine.  
The protagonist comparison is rigged too. You describe Scorsese’s guys in all their specificity and then reduce Nolan’s guys to “troubled geniuses.” Travis Bickle and Jake La Motta are not remotely the same character, sure, but neither are Bruce Wayne and Oppenheimer unless all you mean is “serious men with problems.” Cobb is a liar who has turned his dead wife into a mental prison. Bruce is a rich man trying to make trauma morally useful. Oppenheimer is a political creature who wants the prestige of power and then wants to be mourned for having touched it. Those aren’t flat characters just because Nolan doesn’t have them screaming in a kitchen or beating somebody half to death.  
And the idea that Scorsese looks outward while Nolan only examines himself… Scorsese has spent his entire career circling his own Catholic guilt, his fascination with violent men, his fear of appetite and punishment. That’s not criticism, it’s why his movies feel authored. But pretending those are observations about “the world” while Nolan’s fixations on time and guilt are just neuroses is obviously loaded language. They’re both obsessive filmmakers making the same movie over and over in different forms, which is what most great directors do.

I prefer Scorsese too, but “Nolan doesn’t hold a candle to him” is just fanboy language dressed up as analysis. You can praise Scorsese without pretending Nolan is too shallow to understand that brilliant men can also be pathetic.

## 3. Terminator 2 and Andersen's "The Steadfast Tin Soldier".

**Score:** 11
**Body:** **The ending of *Terminator 2* bears a striking structural resemblance to Andersen’s *The Steadfast Tin Soldier.** 

In Andersen, (https://andersen.sdu.dk/vaerk/hersholt/TheSteadfastTinSoldier_e.html) 
the one-legged soldier is cast into the fire and melts, leaving behind only a small tin heart. The paper ballerina he loves is then caught by a draught and blown into the same flames.

In *T2*, the Terminator likewise ends in fire, descending into molten steel and leaving behind not a heart but the raised thumb: a final, unexpectedly human sign from a being supposedly without feeling. Sarah Connor, meanwhile, has already undergone the ballerina’s death in her nuclear nightmare, where she is trapped against the playground fence, consumed by flame and reduced to a burning skeleton.

The parallel becomes more interesting because Cameron does not simply repeat Andersen. He systematically inverts him.

The delicate, passive paper ballerina becomes Sarah Connor: muscular, armed, furious, and almost machine-like in her discipline. The unfeeling metal soldier becomes the film’s most emotionally affecting figure. Andersen joins the soldier and ballerina in one fire; Cameron separates their immolation into vision and reality, nightmare and sacrifice.

Even Sarah is doubled. Behind the fence, the hardened warrior watches her softer maternal self playing with John. She is both soldier and ballerina, both protector and vulnerable human body.

So the resemblance is not merely “Tin Soldier equals Terminator.” *T2* appears to redistribute Andersen’s tragic pair across Sarah and the machine, then reverse their qualities. The ballerina becomes the warrior; the metal soldier discovers a heart; the domestic stove becomes Judgment Day.

The flaming thumbs-up is the tin heart.

## 5. The Piano Teacher - if Nikki in Obsession was just her true self

**Score:** 0
**Body:** I finally watched this one. The reason why I avoided it whenever I heard it mentioned as something interesting was because I mixed it up with a pretty bad movie I saw as a kid, and thought it was some shitty romance. Then I realized it was from Haneke and got interested. I couldn’t have been more off in my expectations. 

I’m also making this review before I read anything about the movie, because my goal is not to analyze it much at this stage, just to share the strong reaction it left me with. I am very desensitized to most things, but this movie really repulsed me. I say this as a huge compliment, I guess. 

The character of Erika made me very uncomfortable. I can’t say I understand her at all. But what the movie did so well is how it approached her. Just like that guy, we get to see her as a very hot, smart woman, who is a little weird but has her shit together. I found her very attractive in the first half of the movie. Even though we got to see some of her pervy side, I still took it as intriguing, although I thought hat if she wasn’t an attractive woman, a lot of it would be just grotesque. 

But at the point when she revealed her wishes and then started acting so differently, she evoked a true sense of revulsion in me. In a way the movie made me feel exactly like that guy Walter, at first seeing her as someone idealized and then becoming disgusted, although of course that continued in a different direction. It was more effective than most horror movies, how she transformed. I have to give it to the actress. 

In that specific aspect, it reminded me of Obsession, but while I can’t judge Nikki for her behavior caused by practically being possessed, the transformation in Erika is just her revealing her true wishes. As if the premise of Obsession was not that Nikki had to become possessed and incapacitated to act that way, but that the wish unleashed her true inner self and it was like that, and how horrifying would that be. 

But then, how do you engage with that without hating her? I genuinely don’t understand people who are into this kind of shit, so maybe I’m not the best judge, but in a way I got it - if to be with her you have to do the things she wants, and that’s what those things are, how can you not end up thinking of her as repulsive and wanting to hurt her (since that’s what she wants…) 

I am completely confused by the ending. I don’t know if the final act was just Walter doing what she wanted, or if she really got hurt. I don’t really know what she wanted in the first place. The day after makes it seem she is pretty hurt and fucked up, which intuitively makes sense but not according to her logic. Did Walter do anything wrong? I truly have no idea. 

 For me the scene was really hard to watch, but in a weird way where I didn’t feel pity for her but embarrassment. It was so uncomfortable, with her mom there, it gave me that real sense of anxiety and I don’t even know on whose behalf. 

Similarly, the scene where she is trying to sexually assault her mother and they just keep lying next to each other, it’s mental but as bizarre as it is, it’s done so well that I believed it and that made it hard to stand. 

I watched Nymphomaniac before, I liked it a lot, but this movie is one of the most uncomfortable movies I’ve ever seen, and her character genuinely sickened me. I respect the actress for what she pulled off. 

I don’t understand what she wants at the end or why she stabs herself and leaves, what kind of reaction she wanted from him on that occasion. It is weird how a character who makes no sense to me managed to be so believable. 

Overall, a great movie, deserves its reputation. I have no idea what I think of the plot or the characters.
